mainTopic: How a רגל affects people under restrictions: a baby and mourning, an אבל, a מנודה and a מצורע on the festival, and the source that an אבל may not cut his hair.
overview: The amud opens by asking whether a baby counts as a mourner. A ברייתא shows that we tear a baby's clothes only to move the people who see him, so he is not a real mourner. In a second version, שמואל says any baby may get a haircut on the מועד, and רב פנחס's proof for this is pushed aside by רב אשי. Next the גמרא teaches that an אבל does not mourn on a רגל, because the whole community's מצוה of festival joy outweighs one person's mourning. It then asks whether a מנודה keeps his ban on the festival. רב יוסף and אביי argue back and forth over a ברייתא about the court judging on the מועד, and אביי's later proof is rejected by רבא. The גמרא also asks whether a מצורע keeps his practices on the festival, and רבא proves from a כהן גדול that he does. Finally, the גמרא learns from the command to the sons of אהרן that an אבל may not cut his hair.

steps.title: If some babies can't get a haircut, would a baby be a mourner?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that if a baby's haircut on the מועד depends on when he was born, then mourning laws would apply to a baby. But a ברייתא shows we tear a baby's clothes only to stir up grief in others.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say a baby has a difference in law, then mourning applies to a baby. But a ברייתא teaches that we tear a baby's clothes only because of the grief it causes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge. If some babies may not get a haircut on the מועד, the earlier rule would make them keep mourning laws, and a ברייתא suggests that is not true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier rule was understood to mean that whoever may not cut hair on the מועד also may not cut hair during אבלות. So if some babies may not cut hair on the מועד, those babies would keep אבלות. The ברייתא shows a baby is not a real mourner: his clothes are torn only to move the people who see him.

keyTerms.meaning: A distinction or difference in the law
We tear clothes, as a sign of mourning
Grief or sadness of the heart

steps.confusionAlert: The baby's clothes are torn, but that does not make him a mourner. It is done only to move the people around him.

phrases.english: And if you say that a baby
has a distinction in his law,
phrases.notes: The difference is between a baby born before the מועד and one born during it.

phrases.english: it turns out that mourning applies to a minor.
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
We tear the clothes of a minor
because of the grief it causes!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ קָטָן אִית בֵּיהּ פְּלוּגְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of haircuts for a baby on the מועד and the rule linking מועד and אבלות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a baby's haircut on the מועד depends on when he was born, together with the rule that what is forbidden on the מועד is forbidden in אבלות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Put together, these ideas would make a baby keep אבלות. But the ברייתא shows a baby's clothes are torn only to cause grief in others, so he is not a real mourner.

steps.title: רב אשי: the link between the festival and mourning was never stated outright
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the source never said 'these are forbidden' in אבלות. Perhaps some people who may not cut hair on the מועד may still cut hair during אבלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Does it actually teach 'these are forbidden'? Maybe some of them are forbidden and some are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the challenge by questioning its starting point. The rule 'forbidden on the מועד, so forbidden in אבלות' was only an inference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source said only that those permitted to cut hair on the מועד may also cut hair in אבלות. It never said the reverse. So a baby who may not cut hair on the מועד can still be allowed to during אבלות, and he does not become a mourner.

keyTerms.meaning: Does it actually teach...? Asks whether the source really says this

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a reverse inference from a source is not the same as an explicit ruling, and it keeps the conclusion that a baby is not a mourner.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Does it teach 'these are forbidden'?!
phrases.notes: He means the source never said outright that whoever is forbidden on the מועד is also forbidden while mourning.

phrases.english: Perhaps there are some among them who are forbidden
and there are some among them who are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1 by rejecting its starting point.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the reverse inference that what is forbidden on the מועד is forbidden in אבלות.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed that anyone forbidden to cut hair on the מועד is also forbidden during אבלות, which would make a baby a mourner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The source taught only the permitted side. Some people forbidden on the מועד may still be permitted in אבלות, so a baby is not a mourner.

steps.title: Second version: שמואל permits a haircut for any baby on the festival
steps.stepSummary: אמימר, or some say רב שישא בריה דרב אידי, taught it differently: שמואל said a baby may have a haircut on the מועד, whether he was born during the מועד or before it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר, or some say רב שישא son of רב אידי, taught it this way: שמואל said a baby may have his hair cut on the מועד, whether he was born on the מועד or before it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the teaching. In this version, שמואל makes no difference between babies at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the law for a baby depended on when he was born. Here שמואל says every baby may have a haircut on the מועד. So the challenge from step 1 never comes up at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say; introduces another name for the speaker
Taught it this way; a different version

steps.whatToRemember: In this version, שמואל says any baby may have a haircut on the מועד, no matter when he was born.

phrases.english: Ameimar, and some say
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi,
taught it this way.
Shmuel said:
A baby may have his hair cut during the festival,
no matter whether he was born during the festival
or whether he was born before it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר, וְאִי תֵּימָא רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי, מַתְנֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of שמואל's teaching, in which a baby's law does not depend on when he was born.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A baby may have a haircut on the מועד, whether he was born during the מועד or before it.

steps.title: רב פנחס quotes a ברייתא linking haircuts on the מועד to haircuts during mourning
steps.stepSummary: רב פנחס says we have a source supporting שמואל's lenient ruling. He quotes a ברייתא and draws an inference from it: whoever may not cut hair on the מועד may also not cut hair during mourning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פנחס said: We also learned this in a ברייתא. Everyone who is allowed to cut his hair on the מועד is also allowed to cut his hair during his days of mourning. That means those who are not allowed to cut their hair on the מועד are also not allowed during their days of mourning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פנחס brings a ברייתא as support for שמואל's ruling that a baby may always get a haircut on the מועד. This step sets up the source; the proof itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא ties two sets of rules together: haircuts on the מועד and haircuts during אבילות. רב פנחס also reads the rule in reverse: if you are forbidden on the מועד, you are forbidden during mourning. That reversed reading is what the proof will be built on.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have learned it: a formula for bringing support from an earlier source
חול המועד, the in-between days of a festival

steps.confusionAlert: This looks like a repeat of steps 1–2, but it is not. In the first version, this same reasoning was a קשיא against שמואל. In this second version, שמואל rules that a baby is always allowed, so the same ברייתא now works as a proof for him.

phrases.english: Rav Pinchas said:
We too have learned it in a ברייתא:
phrases.notes: This backs up שמואל's ruling that a baby may always get a haircut.

phrases.english: All those about whom the Sages said
that it is permitted to cut hair on the מועד
are permitted to cut hair during their days of mourning.
This implies: those forbidden to cut hair on the מועד
are forbidden to cut hair during their days of mourning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support שמואל's ruling as stated in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's ruling that a baby may have a haircut on the מועד whether he was born before it or during it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא linking haircut permission on the מועד to haircut permission during אבילות, together with its implied reverse.

steps.title: Why a baby must be allowed: a baby does not keep mourning
steps.stepSummary: רב פנחס completes his proof. If a baby were forbidden to have a haircut on the מועד, the ברייתא would make him forbidden during mourning too, which would mean a baby keeps אבילות. But another ברייתא shows that we tear a baby's clothes only to stir up grief in the people around him, not because he is actually a mourner.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say a baby is not allowed to cut his hair on the מועד, then it turns out that mourning applies to a baby. But a ברייתא teaches that we tear a baby's clothes only because it causes grief to those who see it.
steps.whatsHappening: The proof is finished here. If babies were forbidden on the מועד, they would also be keeping mourning, and that cannot be true, so babies must be allowed on the מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a proof by contradiction. Being forbidden on the מועד would lead to the idea that a baby keeps אבילות. The ברייתא about tearing a baby's clothes shows a baby has no real mourning duties, since the tearing is only for the people watching. So the starting assumption is wrong, and a baby may have a haircut on the מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: Grief or heartache, here felt by the people who see the baby

phrases.english: If you say a baby is forbidden to have a haircut on the מועד,
it turns out that mourning applies to a baby.
But it was taught: we tear a baby's clothes
because of the grief it causes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the inference from step 4 to show that a baby must be allowed to have a haircut on the מועד.
steps.raayaObject: A baby may have a haircut on the מועד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that we tear a baby's clothes only to stir up grief in others, which shows that a baby does not keep אבילות.

steps.title: רב אשי rejects the proof
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי points out that the ברייתא only says who is allowed. It never says that everyone forbidden on the מועד is also forbidden during mourning. Some of them may be forbidden and some allowed, so the proof falls apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Does the ברייתא actually teach 'those who are forbidden'? Maybe some of them are forbidden during mourning and some of them are allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי knocks down רב פנחס's proof. The reversed rule it depended on was never written in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole proof stood on the inference 'whoever is forbidden on the מועד is forbidden during mourning.' רב אשי says the ברייתא only states the positive side. A baby could therefore be forbidden on the מועד and still be allowed during mourning, so there is no proof for שמואל. This does not show שמואל is wrong; it only takes away the support.

keyTerms.meaning: Does it actually teach? Used to challenge a reading that adds to the text

steps.whatToRemember: In this version, שמואל rules that a baby may always have a haircut on the מועד. רב פנחס's proof from the ברייתא is pushed aside by רב אשי, because the ברייתא never states the 'forbidden' half.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: מִי קָתָנֵי הָא אֲסוּרִין?
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Does it actually teach 'but those who are forbidden'?
phrases.notes: He's pointing back to the line in step 4 that רב פנחס worked out, but the ברייתא never actually said.

phrases.english: Perhaps some of them are forbidden during mourning
and some of them are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof built in steps 4–5 by attacking the inference it relied on.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof, not שמואל's ruling itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The rule 'forbidden on the מועד means forbidden during mourning' is only an inference, not written in the ברייתא, and it may not hold for every case.

steps.title: A mourner does not keep his mourning on a festival
steps.stepSummary: A new topic begins. An אבל does not keep the practices of mourning during a רגל, because the תורה commands joy on the festival.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mourner does not keep his mourning on a festival, as it says: 'And you shall rejoice in your festival.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new section with a basic rule: mourning stops for the רגל. It also gives the פסוק that is the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה of שמחה on the festival clashes with the practices of mourning, and the festival's joy wins. This statement sets up the next discussion about how the רגל affects mourning.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And you shall rejoice in your festival', the source for the מצוה of joy on יום טוב

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule is the basis for the halacha that public mourning practices are put on hold during יום טוב.

phrases.english: A mourner does not keep his mourning on a festival,
as it says: 'And you shall rejoice in your festival.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of a baby's haircut has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אבל does not keep mourning practices on a רגל, because of the מצוה ״וְשָׂמַחְתָּ בְּחַגֶּךָ״.

steps.title: Why the festival pushes mourning aside
steps.stepSummary: The festival's מצוה of joy belongs to the whole community, so it overrides a mourner's private מצוה. Mourning that would start during the festival also cannot override that joy.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the mourning started before the festival, the community's מצוה comes and pushes aside the individual's מצוה. If the mourning would start now, during the festival, the individual's מצוה cannot come and push aside the community's מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the rule from step 7, that an אבל does not mourn on a רגל. It looks at two cases: mourning that began before the festival, and mourning that would begin during it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Festival joy is an עשה that belongs to the whole community, while mourning is an עשה that belongs to one person. If mourning already began, the community's מצוה wins and pauses it. If the death happens during the festival, the private מצוה has no power to push the festival aside, so the mourning cannot start yet.

keyTerms.meaning: A positive מצוה that belongs to the whole community (here, festival joy)
A positive מצוה of one individual (here, mourning)

steps.whatToRemember: Community joy (עשה דרבים) beats private mourning (עשה דיחיד) in both directions. It pauses mourning that already began, and it holds back mourning that would begin during the festival.

phrases.english: If it is mourning from beforehand
the positive מצוה of the many comes
and pushes aside the positive מצוה of the individual.
And if it is mourning of now
the positive מצוה of the individual does not come
and push aside the positive מצוה of the many.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind step 7's rule that an אבל does not mourn on a רגל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mourning that began earlier is pushed aside by the festival, and mourning cannot begin during the festival, because a communal עשה outweighs an individual עשה.

steps.title: Does a banned person keep his ban on the festival?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a מנודה must keep the rules of his ban during a רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person under a ban: what is the law? Does he keep his ban on the festival?
steps.whatsHappening: Having seen that festival joy pushes aside mourning, the גמרא now asks the same question about a person under נידוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like mourning, a ban involves restrictions that could clash with festival joy. The open question is whether the רגל pushes aside the ban the way it pushes aside mourning.

keyTerms.meaning: A person placed under a ban by the court
A ban: a punishment that cuts a person off socially

phrases.english: One who is under a ban, what is the law
as to whether he keeps his ban on the festival?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the idea that a festival overrides mourning and asks whether it also overrides a ban.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a מנודה must keep his ban during a רגל.

steps.title: The court judges on the מועד and bans those who will not obey
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף brings a ברייתא: on the מועד the court judges capital, lashes and money cases, and it bans someone who refuses to obey the ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Come and hear. The court judges capital cases, cases of lashes and money cases. If a person does not obey the ruling, we ban him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a source to answer the question. This step sets up the source, and the next step draws the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The important detail is that the court places a ban during the מועד itself. רב יוסף will use this to show that a ban must be in force on the festival.

keyTerms.meaning: Cases where the punishment is lashes
We place him under a ban

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: Come and hear:
We judge capital cases
and cases of lashes and money cases,
and if he does not obey the ruling
we place him under a ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to answer the question in step 9.
steps.raayaObject: That a מנודה keeps his ban on the רגל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא saying the court judges on the מועד and bans those who do not obey.

steps.title: If the festival cancelled bans, the court would not ban people on it
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף argues that if the festival pushes aside an old ban, the court could not possibly start a new ban during it. So a ban must stay in force on the festival.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you thought that a person does not keep his ban on the festival: a person who was banned from before has his ban pushed aside when the festival comes. Would we then ban someone now, on the festival?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף finishes his proof with a קל וחומר, a 'how much more so' argument, from the ברייתא in step 10.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An old ban is the stronger case, since it is already in place. If the רגל could push even that aside, the court surely would not start a new ban during the רגל. Since the ברייתא says the court does ban people then, a ban must stay in force on the festival.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you thought: introduces an idea the גמרא is about to show is wrong
Someone who is already under a ban

phrases.english: And if you thought
that he does not keep his ban on the festival,
then for one who was already banned from before,
the festival comes and pushes his ban aside
would we now, on the festival, ban him?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ אֵינוֹ נוֹהֵג נִידּוּיוֹ בָּרֶגֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the actual proof from the ברייתא quoted in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: A ban stays in force during the רגל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר based on the ברייתא: the court would not start a new ban on the festival if the festival cancels even an old one.

steps.title: Maybe the court only looks into cases on the מועד
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that 'judging' may only mean looking into the case, not deciding it, so no ban is actually given on the מועד. Otherwise the court would be carrying out executions on the מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But perhaps it means only looking into his case? For if you do not say so, then in the capital cases it teaches, would we here too put him to death?!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי rejects רב יוסף's proof by reading the ברייתא differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the court only examines cases on the מועד and decides them after the festival, it never bans anyone during the רגל, and the קל וחומר falls apart. אביי backs up this reading by pointing to the capital cases in the same ברייתא. The court surely does not execute anyone on the מועד, so 'judging' there must mean examining only.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps: opens a different possibility that weakens a proof
For if you do not say so

steps.whatToRemember: רב יוסף's proof is rejected because the court may only look into cases on the מועד without deciding them. The question about a מנודה is still open at this point.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not saying a מנודה is free of his ban on the festival. He is only showing that this ברייתא does not prove the answer either way.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
But perhaps it means only looking into his case?
For if you do not say so,
then the capital cases that it teaches,
here too would we put him to death?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: וְדִלְמָא לְעַיּוֹנֵי בְּדִינֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב יוסף's proof from steps 10 and 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: It rejects the proof only; it does not decide the question about a מנודה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא may mean the court only examines cases on the מועד without deciding them, so no ban is ever given during the festival. The capital cases in the same ברייתא show this reading is needed.

steps.title: Judges who execute may not eat that day
steps.stepSummary: אביי supports his rejection: if the court really executed on the מועד, the judges would lose their festival joy, because judges who carry out an execution may not eat that whole day.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the judges would be kept from the joy of יום טוב! As a ברייתא teaches: רבי עקיבא says, how do we know that a סנהדרין that executed someone may not taste anything that whole day? The פסוק says, 'Do not eat over the blood.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the court cannot really execute anyone on the מועד. Judges who carry out an execution are not allowed to eat for the rest of that day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This backs up the end of step 12. A festival day with no eating cannot be a day of שמחת יום טוב. So the ברייתא's 'judging capital cases' cannot mean a real verdict and execution.

keyTerms.meaning: they would be held back from
the מצוה of rejoicing on the festival
the high court that judges capital cases

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא קָא מִימַּנְעִי מִשִּׂמְחַת יוֹם טוֹב —
phrases.english: But they would be held back from the joy of the festival!
phrases.notes: 'They' are the judges. If they executed someone on the מועד, they couldn't celebrate properly.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Akiva says:
From where do we know about a Sanhedrin (that saw one)
phrases.notes: The words in round brackets are in the standard printed גמרא, but the corrected wording leaves them out.

phrases.english: that put a person to death
that they may not taste anything that whole day?
The verse teaches: "You shall not eat over the blood."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא מִימַּנְעִי מִשִּׂמְחַת יוֹם טוֹב דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source behind אביי's claim that the court cannot execute on the מועד.
steps.raayaObject: That a court cannot actually carry out executions on the מועד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי עקיבא, based on ויקרא 19:26: judges who executed someone fast that whole day.

steps.title: Judging on the מועד means only looking into the case
steps.stepSummary: אביי concludes that capital cases on the מועד are only looked into, not decided. The same goes for money and lashes cases, so no ban is given on the מועד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means looking into his case. Here too, it means looking into his case.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his answer to רב יוסף. 'Judging' in the ברייתא means only studying the case, and this applies to all the cases it lists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Capital cases must mean deliberation only, since a real execution would ruin the judges' festival. Once that is so, money and lashes cases also mean deliberation only. That removes רב יוסף's proof that a new ban can be given on the מועד.

keyTerms.meaning: to look into his case (without deciding it)

phrases.english: Rather, it means looking into his case,
here too, it means looking into his case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְעַיּוֹנֵי בְּדִינֵיהּ הָכָא נָמֵי לְעַיּוֹנֵי בְּדִינֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from step 13 and applies it to the whole ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רב יוסף's proof from the ברייתא (step 11).
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב יוסף assumed 'judging' means giving a final ruling. It may only mean deliberating.

steps.title: Delaying the verdict tortures the accused
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף objects: if the court only deliberates and never decides on the מועד, the accused is left waiting in suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If so, you end up tormenting him by holding up his judgment!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף pushes back against אביי's reading. Starting a capital case and not finishing it is cruel to the accused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule against holding up a capital verdict once the case is ready, because the accused suffers while he waits. So reading the ברייתא as 'only deliberating' creates a new problem.

keyTerms.meaning: tormenting him by delaying his verdict

phrases.english: He said to him: If so,
phrases.notes: רב יוסף is speaking to אביי.

phrases.english: you end up tormenting him by delaying his judgment!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִם כֵּן נִמְצֵאתָ מְעַנֶּה אֶת דִּינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's 'only deliberating' reading.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading that the court only looks into the case on the מועד.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Deliberating without deciding leaves the accused suffering, which is not allowed.

steps.title: Deliberate in the morning, rule at sunset
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף shows how the court can finish the case on the same festival day and still enjoy the festival: deliberate in the morning, eat all day, and give the verdict and execute at sunset.
steps.simpleTranslation: They come in the morning and look into his case. Then they go home and eat and drink all day. Then they come back at sunset, finish his case, and execute him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף describes a schedule that solves both problems: the judges celebrate the festival, and the verdict is not held up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the judges have already eaten all day, the ban on eating after an execution costs them nothing. So the ברייתא can mean real verdicts on the מועד. That brings back רב יוסף's proof that a ban can be given, and kept, on the festival.

keyTerms.meaning: they finish his case (give the verdict)

phrases.english: They come in the morning and look into his case,
and go in, and eat and drink all day,
and then come back at sunset
and finish his case and execute him.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as the judges fasting after the execution. By sunset they have already eaten all day, so 'not tasting that day' costs them nothing.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from step 13 and so brings back רב יוסף's proof from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Timing solution: deliberate early, rule at sunset after the festive meal.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Judging on the מועד must mean only deliberating, because executing would cancel the judges' festive eating.
steps.terutzMaskana: The court can give a full verdict on the מועד late in the day, so real rulings, including bans, are possible on the festival.
steps.whyThisMatters: This puts רב יוסף's proof back in play, so אביי now needs a different source to show a ban is set aside on the רגל.

steps.title: A מנודה was allowed a haircut on the מועד
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a new proof: a ברייתא lists a מנודה among those the Sages allowed to cut their hair during חול המועד. This suggests a ban is not kept on the festival.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear: 'And a מנודה whom the Sages permitted.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a new source for the question from step 9, this time trying to show that a ban is NOT kept on the festival.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מנודה normally may not cut his hair. If the Sages let him cut it on חול המועד, that seems to show his ban is set aside during the festival.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:
"And a מנודה whom the Sages permitted!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב יוסף restores his proof, אביי brings a new source for the opposite view.
steps.raayaObject: That a מנודה does not keep the rules of his ban during the רגל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא listing a מנודה among those allowed to cut hair on חול המועד.

steps.title: The Sages permitted 'him', a specific person
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects אביי's proof. The ברייתא says the Sages permitted 'him', which means one specific מנודה whose ban was already lifted, not every מנודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Does the ברייתא say 'that the Sages permitted it'? It says 'that the Sages permitted him.' This is a case where he went and made peace with the person he was fighting with, came before the Rabbis, and they lifted his ban.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes away אביי's proof from the ברייתא about a מנודה cutting his hair on חול המועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי read the ברייתא as a general rule: every מנודה may cut his hair on the מועד. רבא points to the exact wording. 'Permitted him' means one person whose נידוי was cancelled after he made up with his opponent. So the ברייתא says nothing about someone who is still under a ban.

keyTerms.meaning: that they permitted him (one specific person)
he made peace with him, calmed him down
his opponent in the court case

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא allows haircutting only for a מנודה whose ban was lifted. It does not prove that a ban stops on the מועד.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Does it teach "that the Sages permitted it"?
phrases.notes: "Permitted it" would sound like a general rule, as if the Sages allowed haircutting for every מנודה.

phrases.english: It teaches "that the Sages permitted him,"
where he went and made peace with his opponent in the case,
and came before the Rabbis and they released him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof from the ברייתא in step 17.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that a נידוי is not kept on the מועד.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: אביי misread the wording. 'Permitted him' means one person whose ban was already lifted, not a general rule for every מנודה.

steps.title: Does a leper keep his practices on the festival?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a מצורע must keep his צרעת practices during the רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A מצורע: what is the law? Must he keep his צרעת practices on the רגל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new, similar question, this time about a מצורע instead of a מנודה. It is setting up the proofs that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מצורע has restrictions that look like mourning. The joy of the רגל might push them aside. The גמרא wants to know which one wins.

keyTerms.meaning: a person with צרעת, a skin affliction that makes him impure
his צרעת (here: the practices that come with it)

phrases.english: A leper, what is the law
must he keep the practices of his leprosy on the festival?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel question to the מנודה discussion, now about a מצורע.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a מצורע's restrictions stay in force during the רגל.

steps.title: Proof from the נזיר and מצורע who become pure
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a ברייתא: a נזיר and a מצורע who go from impure to pure may shave on the מועד. This suggests that while he is still impure, he keeps his practices.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear: 'And the נזיר and the מצורע who go from their impurity to their purity' may shave on the מועד. This implies that during his days of impurity, he keeps his practices.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tries to answer the question by reading carefully into a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only allows shaving for a מצורע who is becoming pure. אביי infers that a מצורע who is still impure must keep all his practices, even on the רגל.

keyTerms.meaning: a person who took a vow not to cut hair, drink wine, or become impure from the dead
from his impurity to his purity

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:
"And the nazir and the leper
from his impurity to his purity."
This implies: during his days of impurity, he keeps the practices.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer the question of step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That a מצורע keeps his practices on the רגל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that allows shaving only for a מצורע who is becoming pure.

steps.title: The ברייתא uses a 'needless to say' style
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects אביי's inference. The ברייתא may mean that during his impurity, of course he does not keep the practices. It mentions the purification case only because there you might have made a decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is speaking in a 'needless to say' style. Needless to say, during his days of impurity he does not keep the practices. But when he becomes pure, you might think we should make a decree against shaving, in case he delays his offerings. So it teaches us that he may shave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away אביי's proof by reading the ברייתא in the opposite direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumed the ברייתא's silence about the impure days means 'he keeps the practices.' The גמרא says the impure case is so obvious that it did not need to be stated. The purification case was the real חידוש, because the Rabbis might have banned shaving so he would not push off his offerings.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not needed to say; needless to say

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the ברייתא is saying the impure מצורע keeps his practices. The point here is the reverse: in the impure days it is obvious he does NOT keep them, so the ברייתא proves nothing either way.

phrases.english: It is speaking in a "needless to say" style.
Needless to say, during his days of impurity
that he does not keep the practices,
but when he becomes pure, we might decree
lest he delay his offerings,
so it teaches us that he may shave!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof in step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The inference from the ברייתא that an impure מצורע keeps his practices on the רגל.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as 'needless to say.' The impure case was left out because it is obvious that he does not keep them, and the purification case was stated because of a possible decree.

steps.title: Proof from the High Priest who is a leper
steps.stepSummary: רבא proves from 'והצרוע', which includes a כהן גדול, that a מצורע keeps his practices on the רגל. A כהן גדול is treated all year like everyone else on a רגל, since he serves even as an אונן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Come and hear: 'And the מצורע' comes to include a כהן גדול. A כהן גדול is all year like everyone else on a רגל, as we learned: a כהן גדול brings offerings as an אונן but does not eat them. Learn from this that a מצורע keeps his practices on the רגל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a new proof from a פסוק that the תורה applies the צרעת practices even to a כהן גדול.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On a רגל, mourning-type restrictions are set aside so people can serve and rejoice. A כהן גדול is like that all year: he keeps serving even as an אונן. If the תורה still makes a כהן גדול keep his צרעת practices, then a regular מצורע must keep them on a רגל too.

keyTerms.meaning: a mourner on the day of a close relative's death, before burial

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a clear source that a מצורע's restrictions are not pushed aside by the רגל, unlike what one might have thought from festival joy.

phrases.english: Rava said: Come and hear:
"And the leper" comes to include the High Priest.
And the High Priest, the whole year
is like everyone else on a festival,
as we learned: the High Priest brings offerings as a mourner
but does not eat them.
Learn from this: he keeps the practices of his leprosy on the festival.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After אביי's proof was rejected, רבא offers a new proof for the question of step 19.
steps.raayaObject: That a מצורע keeps his צרעת practices on the רגל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'והצרוע' includes a כהן גדול, together with the משנה that a כהן גדול serves as an אונן, showing his whole year is like a רגל.

steps.title: The גמרא accepts the proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts רבא's proof: a מצורע keeps his practices on the רגל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees with רבא's proof and closes the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one pushes back on רבא's proof. The halacha is that a מצורע keeps his צרעת practices even during the רגל.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from it (the proof is accepted)

steps.whatToRemember: A מנודה's haircut ברייתא was about someone whose ban was lifted. A מצורע, however, does keep his צרעת practices on the רגל, as proven from a כהן גדול.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts רבא's proof from step 22.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A מצורע keeps his צרעת practices during the רגל.

steps.title: A mourner may not cut his hair, learned from the sons of Aaron
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא states that an אבל is forbidden to cut his hair. It learns this from the special command to the sons of אהרן, ״ראשיכם אל תפרעו״: they were told not to let their hair grow, which shows that everyone else must let it grow.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mourner is forbidden to get a haircut. We know this because the תורה told the sons of אהרן, "Do not let the hair of your heads grow wild." From that we learn that for everyone else, cutting hair is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic about the practices of an אבל. It states the rule that an אבל may not cut his hair and gives its source in a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After נדב and אביהוא died, their brothers the כהנים were told not to let their hair grow, so they could keep serving. A special command was needed only because the normal mourning rule is the opposite. So every regular אבל must let his hair grow and may not take a haircut.

keyTerms.meaning: A mourner, someone in the mourning period after a close relative dies
The Merciful One, a name for ה׳ used when quoting the Torah
Do not let your hair grow wild (from פְּרִיעָה, long, uncut hair)
By inference; we can work out from this

steps.whatToRemember: An אבל may not cut his hair. The source is the special command to the sons of אהרן, ״ראשיכם אל תפרעו״, which shows that ordinary mourners must let their hair grow.
steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק actually tells the כהנים NOT to grow their hair. Don't think that means mourners should cut it. The logic works the other way: the כהנים needed a special exception, so everyone else keeps the normal rule of not cutting.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the תורה-based source for the well-known rule that an אבל does not take a haircut. The סוגיא builds on it as it discusses mourning practices.

phrases.english: A mourner is forbidden to get a haircut.
Since the Merciful One said to them,
to the sons of Aaron:
"Do not let the hair of your heads grow wild,"
we infer that for everyone else it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic. It moves from the מצורע on the רגל to the rules of an אבל, beginning with the haircut ban.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אבל is forbidden to cut his hair. This is derived by inference from the special command to the sons of אהרן not to let their hair grow.
